Brazilians love covering the Fab Four in all the different styles (from bossa to Tropícalia and MPB), but some intrepid brasileiros prefer to explore other international trends. Melô do Embaixador digs deep into the country’s under-documented history of American soul, funk, and disco, turning up 27 strange and compelling interpretations from 1968 to 2015. Tim Maia, forgotten bandleaders, anonymous studio bands, disco cash-ins, and one-hit wonders all make appearances, some translated into Portuguese, some in instrumental versions, some in endearingly awkward English, and all revealing a parallel history of Brazilian popular music that has largely escaped critical attention. The results range from faithful to bizarre, but they all make a compelling case for hearing these records on their own terms. The Drin :: I Lost My Way for Centuries Posted on August 31, 2026 August 30, 2026 If you make it all the way through to track 21 (of 23), to “Sweet, Sweet Sickly Music”, you’ll hear a tortured guitar unspool against a beat obscured by fuzz. These are hooky songs rotted to phosphorescence, but plodding on nonetheless. The Drin’s tunes live furtively in fetid underground bunkers, where their ear-wormy melodies bounce off muck and concrete. Nighttime :: Looking Glass Posted on August 31, 2026 August 30, 2026 “I can see the future and I can tell you’re smiling,” sings Nighttime’s Eva Louise Goodman on “Mother of Invention,” a quiet confidence in her voice. It’s the centerpiece of her latest album, Looking Glass , which she says is “an album about thresholds. About opening your heart, taking a leap, and coming out on the other side.” Conceived between a previous life in the woods of upstate New York and a move to Los Angeles, where she currently resides, the album is a swirling mélange of dusty psychedelia and cosmic folk music, full of sepia-toned dreamscapes and tinges of western noir. Black Duck with Elena Setién Posted on August 28, 2026 August 28, 2026 The songs are loose-jointed and exploratory, built on repetitive motifs but more than willing to jettison them. The music echoes this liquid aura, full of eddies and cascades, but moving forthrightly towards its goals. Stanley Turrentine & The Three Sounds :: Blue Hour (1961) Posted on August 28, 2026 August 27, 2026 Blue Hour (1961) by Stanley Turrentine & The Three Sounds is a fleeting collaboration that’s perfectly captured by its title. Bondo :: Bondo Posted on August 27, 2026 August 26, 2026 Bondo’s self-titled third album resurrects the glacial, improvisatory spirit of ’90s slowcore and post-rock, channeling Codeine, early Mogwai, and Tortoise through a sound that is at once knotty, menacing, and unexpectedly melodic. The tune is a patient blend of swelling synths, shimmering pedal steel from Rick Pedrosa, and Silverstein’s electric guitar, with a strutting disco undercurrent propelling it all. Transmissions :: Jim James Posted on August 26, 2026 August 26, 2026 Since 1998, Jim James has led My Morning Jacket. It’s his first solo music in eight years, and a killer return to form. Touching on soul, psychedelic pop, folk, and ambient sounds, it’s some of the most spiritual music James has ever recorded, and tellingly, this conversation takes a heady, mystical turn.
